newsitem.title: USA: Key executive's defection requires prompt response.
newsitem.headline: Key executive's defection requires prompt response.

text.p: How should a company respond when a key executive defects to a competitor?
What does the stricken company tell its employees, shareholders, Wall Street and the press? What does it say to the defector? What if the defector possesses trade secrets?
Volkswagen A.G.'s recent agreement to pay $100 million to General Motors Corp. to settle a lawsuit arising from a high-level defection underscores the seriousness of the issue.
In a timely article, Harvard Business Review (Jan.- Feb.) asked legal and personnel experts what they would do if a hypothetical vice president for operations quit unexpectedly to join a competitor.
The experts agreed that the situation calls for a calm and swift response, one that is firm, betrays no anger, and holds out an olive branch.

Kenneth Coleman, senior vice president of administration at Silicon Graphics, Mountain View, Calif., thinks an effort should be made to make the defector reconsider leaving. If it's a matter of money, Coleman says, "consider offering him a compensation package that includes equity."
Since the stricken company will never know the defector's reasons for quitting unless it asks, it should arrange a meeting.
"I've found that most people leaving a company want their departures to be as friendly as possible and are willing to be quite open about what's on their minds," Coleman said.
Attorney Gregory Rubin of Paoli, Pa., thinks company officials should ask the defector to "come back for an exit interview" and, if he declines, "conduct the interview over the phone."

Once communication is opened, the company must make it "absolutely clear" by phone and in writing that the defector "may not use or disclose (the company's) confidential business information," Rubin stressed.

Hal Burlingame, executive vice president for human resources at AT&T Corp., Basking Ridge, N.J., thinks the first step "is to prepare employees for the change and make sure they hear about (the executive's) departure before the press does."

A rush news release should announce the event, "acknowledging (the defector's) contributions, and wishing him well," says Bob Galford, a management consultant on organisational issues in Concord, Mass.
Trade magazines, local newspapers, radio and TV stations all must be contacted promptly.

Coleman believes the defector should be urged to help his former employer out by agreeing to be quoted in the news release as stating, "I'm leaving for personal reasons, but I wish the company all the best" and "I hope for its continued success."

The release's key message, says Stephen Greyser, a director of Edelman Worldwide Public Relations, "should be that the company is committed to continuity" and that its "recent success will not change just because (the executive) is leaving."
Reacting in anger by threatening to sue the defector or extracting "noncompete agreements from current and prospective managers," Greyser said, will only damage the company.

As for suing the defector, Greyser said, a lawsuit would be viewed as "a public sign of retaliation" against him and, possibly, against his new employer. As such, it might trigger "a war" between the rivals that the firm weakened by the defection is not in a position to fight.

Greyser said it would limit the damage if the company could name the defector's replacement quickly to strengthen the "continuity message." But the experts agree it's a mistake to hurry the choice. A poor pick would only compound the damage.
Galford recommends "placing a few calls to important customers" as well as to the media "to tell them personally of the resignation and to show that the company deals well with change."
Shareholders, said Greyser, need to be reassured and the company's chief financial officer "should be prepared to handle a reaction from Wall Street and to field analysts' calls."
One possible public defence is for the company to suggest the talent raid is actually quite a compliment: would a competitor lure away a key official who didn't run a dynamite operation?
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
